title: Percentages, ratios and change
goal: Turn intensity percentages into targets, use heart-rate reserve correctly, and tell absolute from relative change and percentage points from percent.

steps.title: Percent of what?
steps.text:
Training intensity is nearly always a percentage: 75% of [VO2max](g:vo2max), 90% of [FTP](g:ftp), 105% of [critical power](g:critical-power). A percentage is a part divided by a whole, × 100.

The question to ask every time: **percent of what?** Each anchor is a different maximum, measured a different way:

| anchor | measured as |
|---|---|
| % VO2max | oxygen uptake, lab test |
| % HRmax | heart rate |
| % FTP | power, field test |

80% of one is not 80% of another. To turn a percentage into a target, multiply: 90% of a 280 W FTP is 0.90 × 280 = 252 W.

steps.title: Heart-rate reserve
steps.text:
Heart rate doesn't start at zero: the heart is already beating at rest. So a percentage of maximum heart rate sits on top of a big floor.

The [heart-rate reserve](g:heart-rate-reserve) (HRR) removes it: **HRR = HRmax − HRrest**. A target at x% HRR is:

**target HR = HRrest + x% × HRR**

This matters because %HRR lines up with % of VO2 *reserve* (VO2max minus resting [VO2](g:vo2)), almost one-to-one, but not with % of VO2max [[c:hrr-vo2r]]. Percentages only line up when both start from rest.

claims.text: Percent heart-rate reserve matches percent VO2 reserve, not percent VO2max.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, %HRR should not be considered equivalent to %VO2max. Rather, %HRR is equivalent to %VO2R, and this relationship should be used in exercise prescription.
For %HRR versus %VO2R, the mean intercept and slope were -0.1 +/- 0.6 and 1.00 +/- 0.01, respectively, which were not distinguishable from the line of identity.

steps.title: A Karvonen target
steps.problem: A runner's HRmax is 185 beats·min⁻¹ and resting HR is 55. What is 75% of HRR? How does it compare with 75% of HRmax?
steps: 75% of HRR = 0.75 × 130 = 97.5. Add it to resting HR: 55 + 97.5 = 152.5 ≈ 153 beats·min⁻¹.
75% of HRmax = 0.75 × 185 = 139 beats·min⁻¹: 14 beats lower, because it ignores the resting floor.

steps.title: Absolute and relative change
steps.text:
A change can be given two ways:

- **Absolute**: new − old, in the original unit. FTP 250 → 275 W is **+25 W**.
- **Relative**: (new − old) ÷ old × 100. The same change is **+10%**.

Always divide by the **old** value. Dividing by the new one (25 ÷ 275 = 9.1%) is a common slip.

For times, a fall is good: 10 km in 40:00 → 38:00 is −2 min, or −5%. Write the sign so a reader knows which way it went.

steps.title: Percentage points
steps.text:
When the thing that changes is itself a percentage, there are two different "percent" changes.

If gross efficiency rises from 20% to 22%, that is **+2 [percentage points](g:percentage-point)** (22 − 20), but a **10% relative** rise (2 ÷ 20).

Headlines love the bigger number. "Halves injury risk" may mean injuries fell from 6% of runners to 3%: a 50% relative fall, but only 3 percentage points, or 3 fewer runners in every 100.

Good reporting gives both: the absolute difference and the relative change.

points: Every intensity percentage needs an anchor: % of VO2max, % HRmax, % FTP and % CP are different scales.
Target = percentage × anchor: 90% of a 280 W FTP is 252 W.
HRR = HRmax − HRrest; target = HRrest + x% × HRR. %HRR matches %VO2 reserve, not %VO2max.
Absolute change is new − old; relative change divides by the old value.
Between two percentages, percentage points are the plain difference; relative change can sound much bigger.

variants.stem: Cyclist A rides at 80% of VO2max and cyclist B at 80% of HRmax. Are they working at the same intensity?

options.text: Not necessarily: each is a share of a different maximum
options.why: Right: VO2 and heart rate don't line up one-to-one as shares of their maxima, so 80% of each needn't match.

options.text: Yes: 80% is 80% whatever it is a percentage of
options.why: A percentage only means something with its anchor. These are different anchors.

options.text: Yes: heart rate and VO2 both rise in step from zero
options.why: Heart rate is well above zero at rest, so the shares don't match.

options.text: Not necessarily: but only because the riders' masses differ
options.why: Body mass isn't the issue; the problem is the two different maxima used as anchors.

variants.stem: A running plan says "tempo at 85%" with no other detail. What is the first thing you need to know?

options.text: 85% of what: VO2max, HRmax, threshold pace or something else
options.why: Right: each anchor gives a different target, so a percentage without one can't be used.

options.text: Nothing: 85% means the same effort on any scale
options.why: Different anchors (HR, VO2, pace, power) give different efforts at the same percentage.
Mass doesn't turn a percentage into a target; the anchor does.

options.text: Only how long the tempo lasts
options.why: Duration matters for the session, but first you need the anchor to know the target.

variants.stem: A cyclist's FTP is 280 W. An interval is set at 105% of FTP. What is the target power?

options.why: This divides by 1.05 (280 ÷ 1.05). A percentage of FTP is a multiplication.
This adds 5 W instead of 5%. 5% of 280 W is 14 W.

variants.stem: A triathlete's FTP is 250 W. The Ironman bike plan is 72% of FTP. What is the target power?

options.why: This divides by 0.72 (250 ÷ 0.72). A percentage of FTP is a multiplication.
This takes away 28 W instead of 28%. 28% of 250 W is 70 W.

variants.stem: A cyclist's critical power is 320 W. A VO2max interval is set at 110% of CP. What is the target power?

options.why: This divides by 1.10 (320 ÷ 1.1). A percentage of CP is a multiplication.
This adds 10 W instead of 10%. 10% of 320 W is 32 W.

variants.stem: A cyclist's HRmax is 190 beats·min⁻¹ and resting HR is 50. What is 70% of heart-rate reserve?

options.why: This is 70% of HRmax (0.7 × 190), which ignores the resting floor.
This is 70% of the reserve alone (0.7 × 140). Resting HR must be added back.
This adds resting HR to 70% of HRmax (0.7 × 190 + 50), counting the floor twice.

variants.stem: A runner's HRmax is 180 beats·min⁻¹ and resting HR is 45. What is 80% of heart-rate reserve?

options.why: This is 80% of HRmax (0.8 × 180), which ignores the resting floor.
This is 80% of the reserve alone (0.8 × 135). Resting HR must be added back.
This adds resting HR to 80% of HRmax (0.8 × 180 + 45), counting the floor twice.

variants.stem: A triathlete's HRmax is 200 beats·min⁻¹ and resting HR is 60. What is 60% of heart-rate reserve?

options.why: This is 60% of HRmax (0.6 × 200), which ignores the resting floor.
This is 60% of the reserve alone (0.6 × 140). Resting HR must be added back.
This adds resting HR to 60% of HRmax (0.6 × 200 + 60), counting the floor twice.

variants.stem: An exercise test finds that percent heart-rate reserve lines up almost one-to-one with another measure. Which one?

options.why: Right: VO2 reserve is VO2max minus resting VO2. Both start from rest, and %HRR matched %VO2R almost exactly.
%HRR and %VO2max differ, most at low intensity, because VO2max has no resting floor removed.
%HRmax keeps the resting floor, so it runs higher than %HRR at the same effort.
FTP is a power anchor from a field test; it wasn't part of this comparison.

variants.stem: Two cyclists both have HRmax 190 and resting HR 50 beats·min⁻¹. A rides at 75% of HRmax, B at 75% of HRR. Who rides harder?

options.text: A: %HRmax always gives the higher target
options.why: %HRmax ignores the resting floor, so at the same percentage it gives the lower target.

options.text: Neither: the same percentage gives the same heart rate
options.why: The anchors differ: one is 190, the other the 140-beat reserve plus rest.
193 adds resting HR to 75% of HRmax (142.5 + 50), counting the floor twice; it is also above HRmax, which can't be.

variants.stem: Two runners both have HRmax 200 and resting HR 40 beats·min⁻¹. C runs at 60% of HRmax, D at 60% of HRR. Who runs harder?

options.text: C: %HRmax always gives the higher target
options.why: %HRmax ignores the resting floor, so at the same percentage it gives the lower target.

options.text: Neither: the same percentage gives the same heart rate
options.why: The anchors differ: one is 200, the other the 160-beat reserve plus rest.
160 adds resting HR to 60% of HRmax (120 + 40), counting the floor twice.

variants.stem: After a training block a cyclist's FTP rises from 250 W to 275 W. What is the relative change?

options.why: This divides by the new value (25 ÷ 275). Relative change uses the old value.
This reads the 25 W absolute change as a percentage.
275 ÷ 250 = 1.10 is the ratio; the change is 1.10 − 1 = +10%.

variants.stem: A runner's 10 km time falls from 40:00 to 38:00. What is the relative change in time?

options.why: Right: −2 min ÷ 40 min = −0.05.
This divides by the new time (2 ÷ 38). Relative change uses the old value.
This reads the 2-minute absolute change as a percentage.
38 ÷ 40 = 0.95 is the ratio; the change is 0.95 − 1 = −5%.

variants.stem: After an injury a triathlete's critical power falls from 300 W to 285 W. What is the relative change?

options.why: This divides by the new value (15 ÷ 285). Relative change uses the old value.
This reads the 15 W absolute change as a percentage.
285 ÷ 300 = 0.95 is the ratio; the change is 0.95 − 1 = −5%.

variants.stem: After a winter of training, a cyclist's gross efficiency rises from 20% to 22%. How should the change be described?

options.why: Right: 22 − 20 = 2 points; 2 ÷ 20 = 10% relative.
The 2 is percentage points. The relative rise is 2 ÷ 20 = 10%.
The plain difference is 2 points, not 10; 10% is the relative change.
22% is the new level, not the change.

variants.stem: In a triathlon club, the share of members injured each season falls from 10% to 8%. How should the change be described?

options.why: Right: 8 − 10 = −2 points; −2 ÷ 10 = −20% relative.
The 2 is percentage points. The relative fall is 2 ÷ 10 = 20%.
The plain difference is 2 points, not 20; 20% is the relative change.
8% is the new level, not the change.

variants.stem: An ad says a drink "cuts cramp risk by 50%". In the trial, 4% of placebo riders and 2% of drink riders cramped. What is the best judgement?

options.text: True in relative terms, but only 2 fewer riders in 100 cramped
options.why: Right: a 50% relative fall is 2 percentage points in absolute terms; give both.

options.text: It means each rider's cramp risk falls by 50 points
options.why: A fall from 4% to 2% is 2 percentage points, not 50.

options.text: False: the fall is only 2% in relative terms
options.why: 2 is the absolute fall in points; relative to 4%, it is a 50% fall.

options.text: It means half of all riders will stop cramping
options.why: Only 4% cramped to begin with; half of them, 2 in 100, were spared.
